'''''Campsis radicans''''', the '''trumpet vine''',<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | accessdate = 21 December 2017}}</ref> '''yellow trumpet vine''',<ref name="RHS" /> or '''trumpet creeper'''<ref name=GRIN/> (also known in North America as '''cow-itch vine'''<ref name="TvetenTveten2010">{{cite book|author1=John Tveten|author2=Gloria Tveten|title=Wildflowers of Houston and Southeast Texas|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PTTnwfdERq0C&pg=PA184|date=5 July 2010|publisher=University of Texas Press|isbn=978-0-292-78687-5|page=184}}</ref> or '''hummingbird vine'''<ref name="Mayer2010">{{cite book|author=Dale Mayer|title=The Complete Guide to Companion Planting: Everything You Need to Know to Make Your Garden Successful|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=32xpkvpXyvIC&pg=PA246|date=12 November 2010|publisher=Atlantic Publishing Company|isbn=978-1-60138-345-7|page=246}}</ref>), is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the trumpet vine family [[Bignoniaceae]], [[native plant|native]] to eastern [[North America]], and [[Naturalisation (biology)|naturalize]]d elsewhere. Growing to {{convert|10|m|ft|0|abbr=off}}, it is a vigorous, [[deciduous]] woody [[vine]], notable for its showy trumpet-shaped flowers. It inhabits woodlands and riverbanks, and is also a popular garden plant.
==Description==
''C. radicans'' is a vine that climbs on trees, other plants, or structures or trails along the ground and can grow to a length of up to {{convert|10|m|ft|0|abbr=off}}. From the main vine, rigid or woody arching vines up to {{convert|2|m|ft|0|abbr=off}} long extend outward. The plant can form a dense [[groundcover]] or an aggressive [[liana]] covering plants or buildings. The [[leaves]] are opposite and odd-[[pinnate|pinnately]] compound, meaning there is an odd number of leaflets, with one terminal leaflet. 

''C. radicans'' climbs through aerial rootlets and twining stems; these stems grow upwards of 12 m in length.<ref name= "Fact sheet">Wennerberg, S. (2006). Plant Fact Sheet: Trumpet Creeper ''Campsis radicans''. N.R.C.S. United States Department of Agriculture. Baton Rouge, LA. </ref> Its bark is tan in color, and shreds easily.<ref name= "Weakley 2015"> Weakley, A. S. (2015). Flora of the Southern and Mid-Atlantic States. Chapel Hill, NC, University of North Carolina Herbarium. </ref>

Leaves are up to {{Convert|7|in|cm|0|abbr=off|order=flip}} long with 7 to 13 leaflets that are each about {{Convert|3|in|cm|0|abbr=off|order=flip}} long and {{Convert|1.5|in|cm|0|abbr=off|order=flip}} wide. The leaflets are emerald green when new, maturing into a shiny dark green. They are [[ovate (botany)|ovate]] to broadly [[lanceolate]] and the edges are coarsely serrate.<ref name="ANPS">{{cite web |title=Know Your Natives – Trumpet Vine |url=https://anps.org/2022/09/17/know-your-natives-trumpet-vine/ |website=Arkansas Native Plant Society |language=en |date=17 September 2022}}</ref>

===Inflorescences=== 
The flowers come in terminal [[Cyme (botany)|cymes]] of two to eight. Each flower is up to {{Convert|3.5|in|cm|0|abbr=off|order=flip}} long and trumpet shaped. They are orange to reddish orange in color with a yellowish throat and 5 shallow lobes bending backward. They generally appear after several months of warm weather. The flowers have no floral scent. After flowering, a long seed capsule about {{Convert|6|in|cm|0|abbr=off|order=flip}} long appears, eventually splitting in two to disperse its seeds. <ref name="IL">{{Illinois Wildflowers|trees|plants|trumpet_creeper|Trumpet Creeper (''Campsis radicans'')|access-date=2024-07-04}}</ref>

[[File:Pollen of Campsis radicans .jpg|thumb|Pollen under microscope]]

== Taxonomy ==
The botanical parentage of ''Campsis radicans'', as a hardy member of a mostly subtropical group, made its naming problematic: according to [[John Parkinson (botanist)|John Parkinson]], the Virginia settlers were at first calling it a jasmine or a honeysuckle, and then a bellflower; he classed it in the genus ''[[Apocynum]]'' (dogbane). [[Joseph Pitton de Tournefort]] erected a catch-all genus ''[[Bignonia]]'' in 1700, from which it has since been extricated.<ref name="COAT">Alice M. Coats, ''Garden Shrubs and Their Histories'' (1964) 1992, ''s.v.'' "Campsis".</ref>

== Etymology ==
The Latin [[Botanical name#Binary name|specific epithet]] ''radicans'' means 'with stems that take root'.<ref name="RHSLG">{{cite book |last=Harrison |first=Lorraine |title=RHS Latin for gardeners |publisher=Mitchell Beazley |year=2012 |isbn=9781845337315 |location=United Kingdom |pages=224}}</ref> The plant is commonly known as cow-itch vine because skin redness and itching is experienced by some people after coming in contact with the leaves.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Campsis radicans - Plant Finder |url=https://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=277901 |access-date=2021-12-22 |website=www.missouribotanicalgarden.org}}</ref>

== Distribution ==
''Campsis radicans'' is native to the eastern [[United States]] and extreme southern [[Ontario]] in [[Canada]]. It is naturalized in parts of the western United States as well as in Ontario and [[Quebec|southern Quebec]], parts of Europe, and scattered locations in Latin America.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Campsis radicans (L.) Bureau {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:30332621-2 |access-date=2026-07-12 |website=Plants of the World Online |language=en}}</ref><ref>[http://bonap.net/MapGallery/County/Campsis%20radicans.png Biota of North America Program, 2013 county distribution map]</ref>

==Ecology==
In the pre-Columbian landscape, ''C. radicans'' was mostly limited to bottomlands in swamps, but has since become a successful colonizer of thickets, fencerows, and abandoned farmland.<ref name= "Weakley 2015"> Weakley, A. S. (2015). Flora of the Southern and Mid-Atlantic States. Chapel Hill, NC, University of North Carolina Herbarium. </ref> ''C. radicans'' can also be found in floodplain forests, including along their edges, and on river banks.<ref name= "Herbarium">Florida State University Robert K. Godfrey Herbarium database. URL: http://herbarium.bio.fsu.edu. Last accessed: March 2019. Collectors: Jame Amoroso, Loran C. Anderson, Kurt E. Blum, Michael B. Brooks, R. Buchanan, Andre F. Clewell, R. F. Doren, Wm. H. Ellis, Robert K. Godfrey, Norlan C. Henderson, Brenda Herring, Clarke Hudson, Ed Keppner, Lisa Keppner, R. Komarek, Elmo Law, S. J. Lombardo, Karen MacClendon, Sidney McDaniel, Richard S. Mitchell, J. B. Nelson, R. A. Norris, Sara J. Noyes, Kevin Oakes, Elmer C. Prichard, A. E. Radford, Gwynn W. Ramsey, Paul L. Redfearn, Jr., R. R. Smith, Charles S. Wallis, D. B. Ward, S. S. Ward, Roomie Wilson, D. R. Windler, and Jean W. Wooten. States and Counties: Florida: Bay, Calhoun, Columbia, Dixie, Franklin, Gadsden, Gulf, Jackson, Jefferson, Leon, Liberty, Madison, Suwannee, Taylor, Volusia, Wakulla, and Washington. Georgia: Grady. Illinois: White. Kansas: Allen. Louisiana: Lafayette and Tangipahoa. Maryland: Cecil. Mississippi: Jackson and Wilkinson. Missouri: Douglas. North Carolina: Caldwell.  Oklahoma: Latimer. South Carolina: Oconee. Tennessee: Rutherford. Texas: Knox and Taylor.</ref>

The flowers bloom in the summer for about three months<ref name=ncextension>{{Cite web|title=Campsis radicans (Cow-itch, Cow Vine, Devil's Shoestring, Foxglove Vine, Hellvine, Trumpet Creeper, Trumpet Vine) {{!}} North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox|url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/campsis-radicans/|access-date=2024-07-04|website=plants.ces.ncsu.edu}}</ref><ref name=graves2022>{{cite journal|last=Graves|first=Gary R.|title=The ''Campsis''-''Icterus'' association as a model system for avian nectar-robbery studies|journal=Scientific Reports|volume=12|article-number=11936|year=2022|doi=10.1038/s41598-022-16237-9|doi-access=free|issue=1|pmc=9279294}}</ref> and are very attractive to hummingbirds such as the [[ruby-throated hummingbird]],<ref name="IL"/><ref name=ncextension/> while many types of birds like to nest in the dense foliage. [[Halictidae|Halictid bees]], flies, and ants also feed on the nectar of the plant's [[Nectar#Extrafloral nectaries|extra-floral nectaries]].<ref name="IL"/> [[Nectar robbing]] behavior has been observed to be performed by orchard orioles (''[[Icterus spurius]]''), which puncture and enlarge holes in the flower base to access nectaries.<ref name=graves2022/>  Certain [[sphinx moth]]s with elongate [[External morphology of Lepidoptera#Mouthparts|proboscises]] are able to successfully feed on trumpet vines while hovering in front of the flower.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://mdc.mo.gov/discover-nature/field-guide/sphinx-moths-hawk-moths|title=Field Guide: Sphinx Moths (Hawk Moths)|website=Missouri Department of Conservation|access-date=2024-07-04}}</ref>

The flowers are followed by large seed pods.  As these mature, they dry and split.  Hundreds of thin, brown, paper-like seeds are released. These are easily grown when [[Stratification (botany)|stratified]]. Larvae of ''[[Clydonopteron sacculana]]'' (the trumpet vine moth) feed on the seed pods.<ref>{{cite journal |title=HOSTS - The Hostplants and Caterpillars Database at the Natural History Museum |url=https://www.nhm.ac.uk/our-science/data/hostplants/search/list.dsml?searchPageURL=index.dsml&Familyqtype=starts+with&Family=&PFamilyqtype=starts+with&PFamily=&Genusqtype=starts+with&Genus=&PGenusqtype=starts+with&PGenus=campsis&Speciesqtype=starts+with&Species=&PSpeciesqtype=starts+with&PSpecies=radicans&Country=&sort=Family |website=www.nhm.ac.uk| year=2023 | doi=10.5519/havt50xw | last1=Robinson | first1=Gaden S. | last2=Ackery | first2=Phillip R. | last3=Kitching | first3=Ian | last4=Beccaloni | first4=George W. | last5=Hernández | first5=Luis M. }}</ref>

''C. radicans'' occasionally acts as a food source for large mammals.<ref name="USDA Plant Database"> USDA Plant Database [https://plants.usda.gov/core/profile?symbol=CARA2] </ref> However, the plant is slightly toxic if ingested, and contact with flowers and leaves can result in swelling and skin redness.<ref name= "Fact sheet"/>

''C. radicans'' is sometimes considered a weedy species.<ref name= "USDA Plant Database"/> Thinning the vines during the growing season and cutting them back during winter can help to limit their aggressive spread.<ref name= "Fact sheet"/>

==Cultivation==
The trumpet vine grows vigorously. In warm weather, it puts out aerial rootlets that grab onto every available surface, and eventually expand into heavy woody stems several centimeters in diameter. It grows well on arbors, fences, telephone poles, and trees, although it may dismember them in the process. Ruthless pruning is recommended.<ref name="ANPS"/> Outside of its native range this species has the potential to be invasive, even as far north as New England.<ref>{{cite web |title=Campsis radicans (trumpet-creeper): Go Botany |url=https://gobotany.nativeplanttrust.org/species/campsis/radicans/ |website=gobotany.nativeplanttrust.org}}</ref> The trumpet vine thrives in many places in southern Canada as well.

Away from summer heat, ''C. radicans'' is less profuse of flower. A larger-flowered hybrid 'Mme Galen' was introduced about 1889 by the Tagliabue nurserymen of [[Lainate]] near Milan.<ref name=COAT />

The form ''C. radicans'' [[form (botany)|f.]] ''flava'' has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name="RHS">{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Campsis radicans'' f. ''flava''|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/44018/Campsis-radicans-f-flava/Details | accessdate=15 April 2020}}</ref>

A deeper red form "Flamenco" is available.

== Toxicity ==
The plant can cause [[contact dermatitis]].<ref>{{cite web |title=USDA Plants Database |url=https://plants.usda.gov/home/plantProfile?symbol=CARA2 |website=plants.usda.gov}}</ref>
